title: Oppam Grievance Model
subtitle: A simple WhatsApp-and-officer-led grievance flow that cut resolution times from 21 days to 96 hours — without buying a single new piece of software.

gallery.caption: Every grievance, on the Collector's phone within 24 hours.
Walk-ins still welcome — they reach the same queue as WhatsApp.
Weekly pendency review made the model self-correcting.

citizen.summary: Oppam ("with you") is a deliberately low-tech grievance model. You send a message — by WhatsApp, in writing, or in person — and someone in the District Collector's office acknowledges within 24 hours, names an owner within 48, and closes the loop within 96. Most of the time, it just works.
story: When a citizen finds that her pension has been stopped without explanation, the worst outcome is silence. The Oppam model treats silence as the actual failure to be fixed — even more than the original problem.

By committing to four guarantees — acknowledgement, named owner, status visibility, and timed closure — Oppam made the system answer to its own promises, with a level of public visibility that made backsliding politically costly.
changes: A clear single window — WhatsApp number + in-person desk + written letters — all flow into the same queue.
Every grievance gets an acknowledgement within 24 hours with a tracking ID and the named officer who will resolve it.
Citizens can ask for status at any time, and weekly pendency reports are made public at the ward level.
Departments that try to ping-pong cases between themselves are visible in the pendency dashboard — and lose.

overview: The Oppam model started in a single district and asked a hard question: do we actually need a new platform to fix grievance redressal, or do we need to fix the assumptions inside the existing one?

Their answer was to redesign the process, not the technology. A small Collector-led cell consolidated all citizen inputs into one queue, set four hard SLAs, made pendency transparent, and held a weekly cross-department review.

The result is a model that has since been adapted by other districts and departments — and that gives a clear lesson: when the politics of accountability are right, the technology stack required is surprisingly small.

challenges.title: Inter-department ping-pong
challenges.description: Most grievances span more than one department. The default behaviour was to bounce the case sideways. Naming a single accountable owner per grievance broke the loop.

challenges.title: Volume without prioritisation
challenges.description: Without triage, urgent cases (medical, safety) get stuck behind paperwork queries. A simple three-tier severity tag fixed that.

challenges.title: Closure quality vs. closure count
challenges.description: Officers gamed early metrics by closing without resolving. A 30-day citizen call-back audit caught and corrected this.

challenges.title: Sustaining attention after the Collector moves on
challenges.description: Models built on personality fade. Codifying the SOP, dashboards and review cadence made the model survive transfers.

actions: Established a Collector-led grievance cell with full-time staff drawn from existing departments.
Set four guarantees: 24-hour acknowledgement, 48-hour owner assignment, status-on-demand, 96-hour closure (with documented exceptions).
Aggregated all input channels (WhatsApp, in-person, written, helpline) into a single queue with one tracking ID.
Published weekly pendency dashboards at the ward level — with department-wise breakdowns.
Instituted a weekly inter-department review chaired by the Collector to close systemic issues, not just individual cases.
Added a 30-day citizen call-back audit on a random sample to prevent closure gaming.
technology: WhatsApp Business account as primary citizen channel (no new software licences)
Existing departmental email + a shared Google/Excel-based tracker as the queue
Power BI / spreadsheet dashboards published weekly
Helpline numbers integrated with the same tracker by call centre staff
Photo evidence collected on the same WhatsApp thread
outcomes: Average grievance resolution time fell from 21 days to 96 hours.
First-call closure rate reached 92% — most cases resolved without inter-department referral.
Citizen satisfaction (measured on the 30-day audit) reached 87% "resolved and satisfactory".
Three other districts have adopted the model with locally adapted SLAs.
Capital expenditure: zero. The entire model runs on existing platforms and reassigned staff.

processFlow.title: 1. Single window
processFlow.description: WhatsApp + in-person + written + helpline all consolidate into one tracker with a single tracking ID.

processFlow.title: 2. Acknowledgement (24h)
processFlow.description: Grievance cell acknowledges, classifies (severity + department), and confirms tracking ID.

processFlow.title: 3. Owner assignment (48h)
processFlow.description: Single named officer becomes accountable; ping-pong is now visible and culturally costly.

processFlow.title: 4. Resolution (96h)
processFlow.description: Owner closes the loop with the citizen; documented exceptions for genuinely longer cases.

processFlow.title: 5. Pendency dashboard
processFlow.description: Weekly publication at ward / department level; review by Collector with department heads.

processFlow.title: 6. 30-day audit
processFlow.description: Random call-back audit verifies actual citizen satisfaction; closure gaming corrected.

replicationToolkit: Oppam cell job description and staffing template
Four-guarantees SLA document and exception protocol
Single-queue tracker schema (Excel / Google Sheets / Power BI)
Weekly review meeting agenda and decision log template
30-day citizen call-back audit script and scoring rubric
Communication kit: WhatsApp templates, posters, citizen FAQ

timeline.title: Diagnostic
timeline.description: Collector's office audits existing grievance flows — identifies that the bottleneck is process, not tech.

timeline.title: Pilot in one taluk
timeline.description: Four-guarantee SLA tested with full transparency; lessons captured weekly.

timeline.title: District roll-out
timeline.description: Model extended district-wide; departmental review cadence institutionalised.

timeline.title: First call closure crosses 90%
timeline.description: Audit shows actual citizen satisfaction matches dashboard claims.

timeline.title: Adaptation by other districts
timeline.description: Replication toolkit released; three districts adopt locally adapted versions.
